title: Sable and the Weather
premise: Rosalind Okafor has spent her life as a guest in her own family, tuning pianos in other people's houses while her mother's crumbling Victorian waits to be sold. At her mother's funeral, a stranger named Sable greets mourners with an old family name — Whitlock — that Rosalind has never heard spoken aloud. Digging through radiators, deeds, and photographs, Rosalind discovers Sable was the daughter her mother gave away decades ago, and that the house's true ownership was quietly bent to keep her out. As the sale deadline looms, Rosalind must choose between protecting her inheritance and telling the truth; in the end she halts the closing, gives Sable the deed and the name, and finally becomes an owner of something — her own history.
about_author: Paloma Nystrom is a former piano restorer who spent fifteen years listening to old houses before turning to fiction. She writes from a drafty farmhouse in coastal Maine, where she claims every radiator tells her a secret.

chapters.title: The Tuner
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. Establishing her itinerant life tuning pianos across town, her habit of reading houses through their pipes and radiators, and her estrangement from the family home she technically owns but never enters. Emotional beat: quiet displacement — a woman at home everywhere except where she lives.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. At her mother's funeral, a composed stranger in a green coat embraces the family and calls them 'the Whitlocks.' No one corrects her. Rosalind follows her into the churchyard and gets only a first name: Sable. Emotional beat: a hairline crack opens in everything Rosalind assumed about her family.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. Alone in the empty house for the first time, Rosalind tunes the old upright and begins searching its rooms. She finds a sealed radiator vent hiding letters addressed to 'S. Whitlock' in her mother's hand, all returned unopened. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Deed and the Dentist
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. A visit to the county records office reveals the house passed through a man named Edmund Whitlock — not Okafor — and a lawyer confirms the estate paperwork was 'simplified' years ago by her mother's brother, Uncle Gerald. Emotional beat: the dawning sense that belonging was rationed deliberately.

chapters.title: Green Coat
chapters.summary: POV: Sable. The stranger's own account: raised in foster care under the Whitlock name, she found her birth mother two years ago and was turned away at this very door. She came to the funeral uninvited because no one else would say goodbye. Emotional beat: sympathy complicates suspicion — Sable is wounded, not scheming.

chapters.title: Uncle Gerald's Version
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. Gerald, charming and defensive over brandy, insists Sable is a con artist after the house, producing photographs of a woman he claims forged documents. But one photograph is genuinely old — a girl in a green coat on the porch steps, dated before Sable was born. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth begin pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Photograph Album
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. In the attic, Rosalind finds pages cut from the family album and, behind the radiator in the music room, the missing photos: her mother young, holding an infant, with Edmund Whitlock. Her mother had another child, earlier, and buried the whole era. Emotional beat: betrayal reframed as fear — her mother wasn't only cruel, she was cornered.

chapters.title: Closing Date
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. The buyer's attorney pushes to close within the week; Gerald pressures Rosalind to sign fast, before 'that woman' interferes. Sable, meanwhile, has found the returned letters and confronts Rosalind with them, raw with fury. Emotional beat: rising pressure — every party wants Rosalind to decide quickly and wrongly.

chapters.title: The Sale
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. Climax. At the closing table, with Gerald watching, Rosalind reads one of her mother's returned letters aloud, names Sable Whitlock before the room, and refuses to sign until the title history is corrected and Sable's claim acknowledged. Gerald walks out; the deal collapses. Emotional beat: truth chosen over safety, at real cost.

chapters.title: Owner
chapters.summary: POV: Rosalind. Weeks later, Rosalind and Sable sort the house together — the album reassembled, the letters finally delivered. Rosalind transfers half the deed, keeps the piano, and tunes it for the first time for someone who stays. Emotional beat: resolution — belonging earned not by blood or paper, but by telling the truth and staying.
